title: Each Man Gets from His Days What He Has Grown Used To
intro: Al-Barquqi describes al-Mutanabbi reciting to Sayf al-Dawla on horseback in Aleppo. The occasion was the Feast of Sacrifice in 342 AH (954 CE). The poet recalls the capture of Constantine and the escape of his father, the Byzantine commander, before turning to the festival greeting and the demands of princely judgement. In the last movement he pleads a case of his own against rival poets at court.

translation: Each man gets from his days what he has grown used to.
Sayf al-Dawla’s habit is to strike his enemies with the lance.
1.sharh: A maxim about habit turns into the portrait of one man. His title means “Sword of the Dynasty”, yet his characteristic stroke here is a thrust with a spear. Even his name scarcely covers his repertoire.

translation: And he keeps giving the lie to rumours about him,
ending the day better off for what his enemies plan.
2.sharh: The sentence continues the list of his habits. His enemies help make their rumours false when the very preparations they undertake against him put resources within his reach.

translation: Many a man bent on hurting him has hurt himself.
Many a guide has given him the very army he failed to guide.
3.sharh: Two Arabic verbs almost coincide in sound, one for guiding and one for giving a present. Looking back from the army’s defeat, the guide might as well have delivered the whole force as a gift.

translation: Many a proud man never acknowledged God for a moment,
then saw the sword in his hand and professed the faith.
4.sharh: Years of defiance are set against the time it takes to glance at a sword. The observable change is in what the opponent says. The poet lets the sight of the weapon explain the speed of the conversion.

translation: He is the sea. Dive when it is calm
for pearls, and beware of it when it foams.
5.sharh: The pearls and the foam belong to the same sea. A visitor can approach it as a diver seeking wealth, or put himself in the way of its breakers. The prince’s two capacities have one image.

translation: I have seen the sea drown a man by chance.
This man comes for his enemy on purpose.
6.sharh: In Arabic the sea “stumbles” over a man. Al-Wahidi takes that stumble to mean a drowning. The sea has no quarrel with its victim, while the emir chooses whom to strike.

translation: The kings of the earth stay humble before him.
They break with him and perish, or meet him prostrate.
7.sharh: “Leaving” also carries the force of breaking allegiance. The choice the poem gives to men already called kings is stark. They may survive their meeting only in a posture of submission.

translation: His swords and spears bring wealth to life for him.
His smile and open hand kill what they bring to life.
8.sharh: Wealth begins a life in his possession as booty. What implements of war have laboured to acquire can disappear with the effort of a smile and a gift. “Killing” the money means giving it away.

translation: Quick-witted, he sends his hunch ahead to scout for his eye.
Today his heart sees what his eye will see tomorrow.
9.sharh: His judgement is cast as a scout riding ahead of his eyesight. Al-Wahidi takes the subject of “sees tomorrow” to be the eye again. The heart has already reached the same spot a day earlier.

translation: He takes his horses where few can reach.
Were the sun’s rim a pool, he would water them there.
10.sharh: Watering horses is an everyday limit on how far cavalry can go. The poet moves the next watering place right out to the visible edge of the sun and assumes the prince can keep the appointment.

translation: That is why the general’s son called his day a death,
and the general himself called it a birth.
11.sharh: Father and son keep different calendars for one battle. Captivity gives the son reason to call it the end of his life, while escape gives his father another beginning.

translation: You rode by night from Amid to the Jayhan,
three nights’ ride bringing you close and carrying you far.
12.sharh: The address changes to “you” as the journey starts. The opposite verbs measure one ride from its two ends. Its distinction, al-Wahidi observes, is that such distant places can be brought together in three nights.

translation: He fled and gave you his son and his armies,
all of them, with no thought of winning praise.
13.sharh: This is the mock gift first imagined when the guide delivered an army. Praise would ordinarily follow such a lavish donation. The fugitive has given everything under compulsion and has no claim on a donor’s reward.

translation: You came between him and life, between him and his sight.
In you he saw the sword of God unsheathed.
14.sharh: The obstruction is at once mortal and visual. Everything the fleeing commander can see has contracted to a single unsheathed blade. The prince’s title, “Sword of the Dynasty”, rises into a still greater claim.

translation: The blue spearheads sought him alone,
but Constantine became the ransom for his life.
15.sharh: The points of the spears have the intention of the pursuers. Constantine is a ransom in a cruel, retrospective sense, since his capture occupied the men who were after his father.

translation: Fear now makes him put on robes of hair.
He used to pull on bright, linked mail.
16.sharh: The same verb for drawing a garment on serves for the monk’s coarse cloth and the soldier’s polished mail. The poet makes a whole reversal of life turn on the change in what touches the skin.

translation: A stick walks him round the monastery in penitence.
Once even the pace of a sleek chestnut dissatisfied him.
17.sharh: The walking stick takes the active part in the Arabic, as if it led the man. He used to find the gait of a fine horse too slow. Now a stick sets his pace in the short circuit of a monastery.

translation: He repented only when the charge had left his face
wounded, and battle dust had inflamed his eyelids.
18.sharh: Two marks of the battlefield enter the supposed convert’s retreat with him. The last suggested motive for the religious transformation is the very physical memory of a wounded face and sore eyes.

translation: If turning monk could save a man from Ali,
kings would turn monks in pairs and one by one.
19.sharh: Ali is Sayf al-Dawla’s own name. The poet tries the Byzantine commander’s escape on every king at once and imagines the incongruous procession that would result if monastic vows secured immunity.

translation: After that, every man in east and west
is getting a black hair shirt ready for himself.
20.sharh: The uniform of retreat becomes an article of advance preparation. Al-Wahidi limits the deliberately vast “everyone” to those who have reason to fear the prince. The black garment carries the previous verses’ story with it.

translation: Joy to you on the feast whose own feast you are,
a feast to all who name God, sacrifice and celebrate.
21.sharh: This is the first explicit festival greeting. Naming God at the slaughter identifies the Feast of Sacrifice, while the prince himself is made a source of celebration even to the festival personified.

translation: May feast days always be the clothes you wear,
worn through when you hand them in, fresh when they are given.
22.sharh: A festival normally lasts a day. Made into a garment, it can be worn until another replaces it. The wish for an unbroken supply of new clothes is a wish for the prince to live to see many more feasts.

translation: This day among days is like you among people.
As you stand alone among them, so does it.
23.sharh: The comparison runs through two whole populations, days on one side and people on the other. Repeating the same word for uniqueness makes the holiday the prince’s equal within its own kind.

translation: Such is fortune. One eye may surpass its fellow,
and one day become master over another.
24.sharh: Even two eyes set in the same face need not enjoy equally good sight. Good fortune can distinguish near-identical things, just as one daylight period can be singled out for an entire community’s festival.

translation: How strange that a ruler should wear you as his sword.
Does he take no care for the two edges at his side?
25.sharh: The commentators hear an allusion to the caliph in the ruler who wears this “Sword of the Dynasty”. A title of service becomes a real two-edged blade, close enough to endanger its nominal owner.

translation: Whoever takes a lion for his hunting hawk
gets taken by the lion among the game.
26.sharh: A falcon is trained to return to its handler. A lion enlisted on the same terms may include its handler in the quarry. The reversal completes the warning implicit in the sword’s two edges.

translation: I have seen pure forbearance in you, with power to spare.
You could have made your answer a blade of Indian steel.
27.sharh: Restraint means something because the unexercised alternative is within reach. The phrase “pure” is applied to power as well as to forbearance, allowing no admixture of helplessness in the decision.

translation: Nothing kills free men like forgiving them.
Yet where will you find a free man who remembers a favour?
28.sharh: “Killing” is the end of a proud man’s independence when pardon puts him in another’s debt. The second half doubts whether everyone so treated has the character to remember the hand extended to him.

translation: Honour a noble man and he is yours.
Honour a base man and he rebels.
29.sharh: The prince does precisely the same thing twice. The two men supply the difference in outcome. That makes the preceding verse’s uncertainty about the recipient a practical problem of judgement.

translation: Giving where the sword belongs harms high standing
as much as using the sword where a gift belongs.
30.sharh: Two mismatched actions occupy matching places in the verse. This balance makes generosity capable of doing damage too. The prince must discern what the occasion and the recipient require.

translation: But you excel others in counsel and in judgement
as in estate, in spirit and in descent.
31.sharh: After three lines that could sound like advice, “but” changes the speaker’s position. He acknowledges that the man being advised already leads others in precisely the faculty those decisions need.

translation: What you do is too subtle for minds to grasp.
What stays hidden is passed over, what shows is taken up.
32.sharh: Al-Wahidi hears the difficulty as that of the poets selecting their material. The verse acknowledges a limit to praise just before the speaker begins to press his own very particular claim to be heard.

translation: Put my enviers to shame and rid me of their envy.
You are the one who gave them cause to envy me.
33.sharh: Favour created a problem only the giver can solve. The poet makes his rivals’ envy further proof of how much the prince has done for him, even as he asks for public support against them.

translation: When your judgement of them lends my wrist strength,
I strike with a sword that cuts heads in its sheath.
34.sharh: Al-Barquqi reads the prince’s judgement as his withdrawal of favour from the enviers. Once the court sees them lose his backing, the poet can strike with a weapon he never even draws.

translation: I am only a fine spear you have taken up,
an ornament carried crosswise, a terror levelled.
35.sharh: The direction in which a spear is held changes its office without changing the spear. A poet at court can lend distinction in repose and turn his tongue on a patron’s antagonists.

translation: Time itself is one of the transmitters of my poems.
When I speak verse, Time takes it up and recites.
36.sharh: A transmitter preserves somebody else’s words. The poet assigns an age full of speakers this secondary role and reserves the first utterance for himself. The next verses show how many voices the claim embraces.

translation: It sends the stay-at-home briskly on the road,
and one who never sings gives it a ringing voice.
37.sharh: His lines move the person who ordinarily stays put and draw song from someone unused to singing. The two reversals make the circulation of verse audible and visible in ordinary bodies.

translation: Reward me when anyone recites verse to you.
The praise poets bring you is my poetry repeated.
38.sharh: The passive verb leaves the performer unnamed. Whoever gets up to recite, this poet says the fee should come to him because the competitors have brought back his own inventions.

translation: Set every voice but mine aside.
I am the caller they imitate. The other is the echo.
39.sharh: An echo may arrive from another direction and sound like a second voice. Once the listener recognises the source, the pretender to authorship disappears. The prince is asked to listen with that distinction in mind.

translation: I leave night journeys behind to those who lack money.
With your bounty I shoe my horses in gold.
40.sharh: Poor poets still have to travel overnight to reach a patron. This one can put gold beneath his horses’ feet, where travel would ordinarily wear down a much cheaper metal.

translation: I have bound myself to your shelter out of love.
Whoever finds a bond in kindness lets it hold him.
41.sharh: He has the means to travel and chooses to stay. The reflexive “I bound myself” gives the earlier talk of gratitude as bondage a personal test. This tie is one he has put on for love.

translation: Whenever a man asks his days for wealth,
however far away you are, they set a meeting with you.
42.sharh: Days now answer a petitioner in their own person. The opening maxim about what one can expect from time has acquired an exceptionally precise address, wherever this prince may happen to be.

1.1.4.head: دَهر
1.1.4.meaning: A lifetime and the turns of fortune it brings.

1.2.1.head: عادَة
1.2.1.meaning: A customary practice. The reciter gives the singular. Al-Wahidi, al-Ma'arri and al-Barquqi print the plural, “habits”.

1.2.2-3.head: سَيف الدَّولَة
1.2.2-3.meaning: Sayf al-Dawla, “Sword of the Dynasty”, the title of Ali ibn Abd Allah ibn Hamdan, emir of Aleppo.

2.1.3.head: إِرجاف
2.1.3.meaning: Spreading alarming reports to shake people’s confidence.

3.2.1.head: هادٍ
3.2.1.meaning: A guide who shows an army the way.

3.2.4.meaning: Presented a gift. The defeated troops become their guide’s unwitting present.

4.2.5.head: تَشَهَّدَ
4.2.5.meaning: To utter the profession of faith.

5.2.6.head: مُزبِد
5.2.6.meaning: Foaming at the surface as rough water breaks.

6.1.4-5.head: عَثَرَ بِهِ
6.1.4-5.meaning: “Stumbles upon him”, bringing someone to grief by chance.

7.2.2.meaning: Lost or dead, a plural describing ruined kings.

8.1.5.head: قَنا
8.1.5.meaning: Lances, named for the shafts from which they are made.

9.1.2.head: تَظَنٍّ
9.1.2.meaning: Divining what will happen from signs, before the eye has evidence.

9.1.3.head: طَليعَة
9.1.3.meaning: A scout who rides ahead to see what an army will meet.

10.2.3-4.head: قَرن الشَّمس
10.2.3-4.meaning: “The sun’s horn”, the edge of its visible disc.

10.2.6.head: أَورَدَ
10.2.6.meaning: To lead animals to a watering place.

11.1.4.head: الدُّمُستُق
11.1.4.meaning: Domestikos, a Byzantine military title. Here it designates the captive Constantine’s father.

12.1.3.head: جَيحان
12.1.3.meaning: Jayhan, the Ceyhan River in southern Turkey.

12.1.6.head: آمِد
12.1.6.meaning: Amid, the city now called Diyarbakir, on the Tigris.

13.1.4.head: جَيش
13.1.4.meaning: Armies. The plural on the recording’s card adds the commander’s forces to the son he left behind.

14.1.5.head: طَرف
14.1.5.meaning: Eyesight, or what the eye can take in.

15.1.3-4.head: زُرق الأَسِنَّة
15.1.3-4.meaning: “The blue spearheads”, points with the dark glint of polished metal.

15.2.2.head: قُسطَنطين
15.2.2.meaning: Constantine, the Byzantine commander’s son captured on this expedition.

16.1.2.head: اِجتابَ
16.1.2.meaning: To slip oneself into a garment.

16.1.3.head: مِسح
16.1.3.meaning: Coarse garments of haircloth worn by ascetics.

16.2.4-5.head: الدِّلاص المُسَرَّد
16.2.4-5.meaning: Bright armour whose rings have been linked into mail.

17.1.3.head: عُكّاز
17.1.3.meaning: A walking stick, sometimes fitted with an iron point.

17.2.5-6.head: أَشقَر أَجرَد
17.2.5-6.meaning: A chestnut horse with a fine, short coat.

18.2.4.head: النَّقع
18.2.4.meaning: Dust raised by horses in battle.

19.1.5.head: عَليّ
19.1.5.meaning: Ali, the given name of Sayf al-Dawla.

19.2.3-4.head: مَثنى وَمَوحَد
19.2.3-4.meaning: In twos and singly. The distributive in the dictionaries is mawhad. The vowel on the recording sounds closer to mawhid.

20.2.5.head: الشَّعر
20.2.5.meaning: Animal hair woven into a coarse religious habit.

21.2.1.head: عيد
21.2.1.meaning: And a feast. The initial wa means “and”. The emir himself is a feast to the celebrants, the third appearance of the same noun in the verse.

21.2.3.meaning: Invoked the name of God before sacrificing.

21.2.5.head: عَيَّدَ
21.2.5.meaning: To keep a feast day. Naming God, offering a sacrifice and celebrating are the worshipper’s three acts in this line.

22.1.4.head: لُبس
22.1.4.meaning: Something worn, here one feast day replacing another like changes of clothing.

24.1.2.head: الجَدّ
24.1.2.meaning: Good fortune or an allotted share of it.

25.1.4.head: دائِل
25.1.4.meaning: A ruler who has the upper hand in fortune’s turn. The commentators understand the caliph.

25.2.3.head: شَفرَة
25.2.3.meaning: The two keen edges of a sword.

26.1.3.head: ضِرغام
26.1.3.meaning: A lion, here a hunter no one can keep under command.

26.1.4.head: باز
26.1.4.meaning: Baz, a hawk trained for hunting.

27.2.6.head: مُهَنَّد
27.2.6.meaning: A blade of Indian steel, proverbial for quality.

28.2.6.head: يَد
28.2.6.meaning: A favour remembered as the hand that bestowed it.

29.1.5.head: مَلَكَ
29.1.5.meaning: Won his allegiance. The literal language of taking possession measures the hold an honourable benefactor gains.

30.1.2.meaning: Generosity, particularly the gift through which it is shown.

32.1.1-3.head: دَقَّ عَلى الفِكر
32.1.1-3.meaning: “Too fine for thought.” The reasoning behind the prince’s act escapes even the poets trying to describe it.

33.1.5.head: كَبت
33.1.5.meaning: To confound opponents and frustrate their designs.

34.1.3.head: زَند
34.1.3.meaning: The wrist or lower forearm, the point where a hand is braced.

34.1.4-6.meaning: “Your sound judgement of them”, meaning the poet’s enviers. The recording ends the phrase with an i sound where al-Barquqi’s text has u. Al-Wahidi gives a different phrase, “in my hand”.

34.2.4.head: هام
34.2.4.meaning: Heads, or the crowns of heads.

35.1.4.head: سَمهَرِيّ
35.1.4.meaning: Samhari, a straight, strong spear traditionally associated with a maker named Samhar.

36.1.6.head: قَصيدَة
36.1.6.meaning: My poems. Al-Tha'alibi quotes this reading. The video card and the main text of al-Wahidi and al-Barquqi have “my necklaces”, comparing poems to strings of jewels. Al-Barquqi also records “my poems” as a variant.

37.1.6.head: مُشَمِّر
37.1.6.meaning: With his clothes hitched up, ready to stride out.

38.1.1.head: أَجِز
38.1.1.meaning: Award me the customary reward for verse recited before a patron.

39.2.3.head: مَحكِيّ
39.2.3.meaning: Whose voice is reproduced by others.

41.1.4.head: ذَرى
41.1.4.meaning: Shelter or protection afforded by the prince.

42.2.4.head: جَعَلَ
42.2.4.meaning: “They appoint you”. The agents are the days to which the man addressed his request.
